title: The Fed - Supervisory Policy and Guidance Topics - Capital Adequacy
summary: This Federal Reserve webpage serves as a topical index of supervisory policy letters, guidance documents, and manual references related to bank capital adequacy regulation. The page organizes resources across several categories including Basel Capital Accords, Advanced Approaches, Risk-Based Capital Rules, securitization, risk-weighted assets, and regulatory capital treatment. No new policy announcements or specific capital requirements are presented on this page.
key_points: Page functions as a regulatory guidance index/hub for capital adequacy topics, not a standalone policy document
Covers multiple regulatory frameworks: Basel I/II/III capital accords, Advanced Approaches, and Community Bank Leverage Ratio Framework
Includes references to stress testing guidance (SR 12-7) for banking organizations with assets over $10 billion
Lists guidance on risk transfer considerations and consolidated supervision for large financial institutions
Contains interagency statements including FFIEC joint statements on LIBOR transition and capital/liquidity buffer usage
Last updated April 20, 2026, indicating active maintenance of regulatory guidance catalog
why_it_matters: This page aggregates the regulatory framework governing bank capital requirements, which influences bank leverage constraints and risk-taking behavior. While not providing new policy, it serves as a reference for understanding the supervisory expectations that shape bank capital planning and ultimately affect credit availability and market structure. Researchers tracking regulatory evolution in capital standards can use this as a navigation hub.
market_structure_context: The guidance listed here governs bank capital requirements which are foundational to market structure as they determine leverage limits, risk appetite, and the buffer between bank balance sheets and potential losses. The referenced SR 13-23 on risk transfer and consolidated supervision frameworks directly relates to how large financial institutions are supervised and their systemic footprint managed.
